title: Data-Driven and Cycle-Agnostic Covariate Selection for Nonparametric Causal Effect Estimation
claim: Realistic systems contain feedback loops and latent confounding, so covariate selection for causal effects must handle cyclic causal graphs.
layout: single panel, five circular nodes in a triangle-like arrangement, directed arrows, one cycle
description: A single black-and-white causal graph on a white background. Five circular nodes carry italic math labels. LS (lifestyle) sits at the top center. HI (health indicators) and SE (socioeconomic status) sit at mid-left and mid-right. The treatment X and the outcome Y sit at bottom-left and bottom-right. Directed arrows run LS→HI, HI→SE, SE→LS, HI→X, HI→Y, SE→X, SE→Y and X→Y. LS→HI→SE→LS forms a feedback cycle at the top. Two diagonal arrows from HI and SE to Y and X cross in the middle. The eye goes first to the top triangle and the crossing arrows. There is no color and no legend, and the caption defines the abbreviations.
caption: A causal graph of a health care setting. $LS$ represents lifestyle, $HI$ health indicators, $SE$ socioeconomic status, $X$ the treatment and $Y$ the outcome.
abstract: Estimating causal effects from observational data requires identifying valid adjustment sets. This task is especially challenging in realistic settings where latent confounding and feedback loops are present. Existing approaches typically assume acyclicity or rely on global causal structure learning, limiting applicability and computational efficiency. In this work, we study a local, data-driven method for covariate selection based on conditional independence information under a pre-treatment assumption. While this method is known to be sound and complete in acyclic causal models, its validity in the presence of cycles has remained unclear. Our main contribution is to show that these guarantees extend to cyclic causal models. In particular, our result relies on the invariance of conditional independence assertions under $Ï$-acyclification. These findings establish a unified, cycle-agnostic perspective on covariate selection, which allows for causal effect estimation using any consistent estimator. Therefore, showing that the method applies across cyclic and acyclic settings without modification. Empirically, we validate this on extensive synthetic data, showing reliable performance in cyclic causal models.
